newsitem.title: USA: New products - Drake's cakes move into 21st century.
newsitem.headline: New products - Drake's cakes move into 21st century.

text.p: To children growing up on Long Island, N.Y., Drake's cakes were an intrinsic part of life -- from lunch boxes to after school snacks.
Ring Dings, Devil Dogs, Yankee Doodles and Yodels were as well known to Baby Boomers as Snapple and Famous Amos are to today's youth.

The makers of Drake's snack cakes have decided to meet the 21st century head on, by introducing new products, expanding distribution and doing something they have done only sporadically through their 108 year history -- advertise.
After decades of a farly stable product list, Drake's is accelerating its introduction of new products.

In the next month, Drake's plans to introduce three new cakes -- creme pockets, chocolate iced cupcakes and chocolate chip crispy snacks. The new products have a target audience of children aged six to 17.

By the end of the year, the company expects to have introduced 16 new products or line extensions, for a total of 60 snack food products. Next year, Drake's expects to introduce about 15 new products.
This new wave will include low and reduced fat versions of Devil Dogs, Yankee Doodles and Sunny Doodles.
"The trend is toward more healthy -- low and reduced fat," perhaps including more fruit snacks, Vanessa Maskal, vice president of marketing, said.
Drake's fans need not worry, however. "Chocolate is a primary focus," she said.
Prices, too, will hold stable. Drake's prices have not changed much in the last three years, Maskal said. The average price for a box of about eight snack cakes runs from $1.99 to $2.99.

While there is an ever growing market for low and reduced fat snack items, Maskal doesn't believe they will ever be as great sellers as full fat snacks. Currently the market share for low fat snacks is about 1 percent of the fresh baked goods market.
It's time, says Marketing Manager Anthony Patelli, to get a new look, while escalating the introduction of snack cakes.
A major part of Drake's image change will come from new packaging, developed by Sterling Group, a New York-based brand identity and strategic marketing group.
"We wanted to create packaging that is still recognisable to current users, but also introduce the brand to a whole new generation of consumers," said Debbie Millman, senior vice president.

Webster the duck, whose profile has graced Drake's packages for 90 years, will now be seen full face, holding a mixing spoon. The new Webster will appear on Drake's packages, trucks and store displays.
Packaging "is the last five minutes of marketing," Millman said, explaining that if the package is dramatically different, shoppers may not recognise it and buy something else.

The brand is currently distributed throughout the Northeast, but is making inroads in Florida, Tennessee and Arizona. Drake's expects to enter California in February, and fill in marketing holes back East.

Drake's is dipping it's toes gingerly into the water of advertising, Maskal said, after an absence since 1989. It has only sporatically advertised before that. The company will start with radio spots in its major markets.

The brand has had a lot of free adverting in the past year, as a snack of choice for television talk show host Rosie O'Donnell. It's also eaten on sit-coms "Seinfeld" and "The Nanny." Because of the publicity, Drake's said its sales rose 7 percent last year alone.

Since it is privately held, ad budgets are kept secret. However, the company said that the 1996 and 1997 marketing budgets will be 10 percent to 11 percent of sales. It took in about $150 millionto $200 million in sales last year.
Drake's was born in Brooklyn, N.Y., when Newman E. Drake developed a pound cake recipe in 1888. He and his brothers opened the first Drake bakery in 1896.
After moving from family hands, Drake's is now owned by the Montreal-based Culinar Inc., whose Joe Louis snack cakes are major sellers in Canada.
Based in Wayne, N.J., Drake's employs 210 people.
